newsitem.title: USA: 23 million kids had gaps in health insurance - study.
newsitem.headline: 23 million kids had gaps in health insurance - study.

text.p: An estimated 23 million children in the United States lacked health insurance for at least a month in 1995-96, of whom almost half were uncovered for a year or more, a healthcare consumer group said Thursday.
The Families USA Foundation, in a study based on U.S. census data, said most of the one-in-three children who had lacked health insurance during the two-year period lived in working families.
Sen Edward Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat, said the report would give new momentum to congressional efforts to ensure that children have health coverage.
Ron Pollack, executive director of Families USA, called the lack of coverage "an epidemic."

"America's uninsured children live in families where the breadwinners work hard, pay taxes and play by the rules," he said. "But they don't get health coverage on the job, for themselves or their children. And they can't afford to pay for it out-of-pocket."
The study showed that 47 percent of the uninsured children lacked coverage for one month or more during the two-year period and 15 percent were without insurance for the full two years.

Nine of 10 children who lacked insurance lived in households where the head of the household worked all or part of the two years, and nearly two of five household heads where children were uninsured for the full two years were employed fulltime throughout the period.
The study found that 34 percent of the uninsured children lived in families with an income of at least $28,000.

States in the South and West had the highest proportion of children without health coverage, including Texas, with 46 percent, New Mexico and Louisiana 43 percent, Arkansas 42 percent and Mississippi 41 percent.

Senate Democrats have made the child insurance issue their top health priority. President Clinton's balanced budget plan includes incentives to expand insurance to as many as five million children, mainly through extending Medicaid coverage. There is some question whether the plan would be effective.

Kennedy and Utah Republican Sen. Orrin Hatch have introduced a bipartisan bill that would provide grants to states to cover uninsured childen. The measure would be funded by a huge increase in the federal tobacco tax.

House Republicans have endorsed the idea of extending health care to children, but say they want to find a market-based solution. A House Ways and Means subcommittee plans a first hearing on the issue early next month.

"So far, the issue of children without health insurance coverage has generated a significant amount of heat, but very little light. We need to begin this discussion with a better understanding of the scope of the problem before we advocate solutions," California Republican Representative Bill Thomas said in announcing the hearing last week.
